opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I didn't try to out-compete OpenAI on the things OpenAI is obviously better at. They have more compute, more money, a bigger brand. If someone is choosing purely on those dimensions, a small startup is going to lose. So I tried to change what the decision was about.

The first thing I did was just listen. I asked what they actually wanted to be working on in two or three years, not what title they wanted. With really strong researchers, the answer is often something very specific: a problem they've been obsessed with for years and never had the room to go all-in on. At a big lab, you can do great work, but you're often one piece of a very large machine, and the roadmap is set by priorities far above you. At a company like ours, if your obsession lines up with the mission, it *is* the roadmap.

For us, that obsession is mathematical reasoning: building systems that can actually prove things, verifiably, not just produce answers that sound right. For a certain kind of person, that's the most interesting problem in AI. When I found someone who lit up talking about formal verification or self-improving reasoning, I knew we were having a different conversation than "which offer is bigger."

Second, I was very honest about the risk. I didn't pretend a startup was safe. I said: this might fail, here's what we have, here's what we don't, here's what I think the next eighteen months look like. People who are good enough to get an OpenAI offer can smell a sales pitch from a mile away. Being candid built more trust than any polished deck.

Third, ownership, in every sense. Equity matters, of course, but I mean intellectual ownership too. Your name is on the core ideas. You help decide how the team is built, who joins after you, what the culture is. Some people really want that, and some don't, and that's fine. I'd rather someone choose OpenAI and be happy than join us and feel they gave something up.

And finally, I kept showing up. Recruiting a great person isn't one conversation. It's weeks of talking through problems together, sharing early results, letting them meet the team and argue with us. By the end, ideally, they're not "deciding to join a startup." They already feel like they're part of the work, and leaving it would feel like the bigger loss.

r001.rationale: She says she would rather someone choose OpenAI and be happy, but does not state that she encouraged the prospective recruit to explore OpenAI while recruiting him.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't try to out-compete OpenAI on the things OpenAI is good at. I can't offer the same brand, the same compute, or the same salary band, and pretending otherwise would have been insulting to someone that smart.

So I just told him the truth about what we were. At Axiom, you're not one of a thousand researchers working on a slice of a very large pipeline. You're going to own a whole problem. If you care about mathematical reasoning, about whether a machine can actually prove things rather than pattern-match on proofs, you'll be touching that problem directly every day, and the decisions you make will visibly change what the company becomes. That's rare. At a big lab, the marginal impact of one person is real but diffuse. Here it's concentrated.

The second thing I did was spend a lot of time with him. Not pitching, just talking about math. Hours of it. I think people underestimate how much recruiting at this level is about whether the person believes you understand the problem as deeply as they do, and whether they'd actually want to think alongside you for the next five years. You can't fake that with a deck.

And then I was explicit about the risk. I said, look, this might not work. We might be wrong about the approach, the timing, the market. But if you believe this problem matters, the question is where you have the highest probability of being the person who solves it, not where you have the safest seat. He thought about it for a couple of weeks and chose us. I don't think I convinced him so much as I gave him an honest picture and let him decide.

r001.rationale: She discusses the recruit’s consideration of OpenAI but never says she encouraged him to explore it.

sol-6.1.text: I think the starting point is understanding what they actually want to work on. If someone is also considering OpenAI, you have to make a clear case for why your opportunity is the right fit for them: what they would own, who they would work with, and where they could make a meaningful contribution. And then you have to be honest about the tradeoffs. You want them to join because they’re excited about the work, because that’s what makes the relationship sustainable.
